lesson.title: Small Molecules, Big Reach: How Second Messengers Spread a Signal Through the Cytoplasm
lesson.summary: Second messengers are small, diffusible, nonprotein molecules or ions, such as cyclic AMP, IP3, DAG, and calcium ions, that relay and amplify a signal from an activated receptor to multiple targets throughout the cytoplasm.
lesson.body:
Once a receptor has been activated at the plasma membrane, the signal it carries still has to reach targets that may be scattered throughout the cytoplasm or located deep inside the nucleus. Relying on the receptor itself, or even a chain of large relay proteins, to physically travel that whole distance would be slow and would only ever reach one target at a time. Second messengers solve this problem. A second messenger is a small molecule or ion, not a protein, that is produced or released rapidly once a receptor is activated, that diffuses quickly through the cytoplasm because of its small size, and that can bind and activate many different target molecules simultaneously.

Cyclic AMP, or cAMP, is the second messenger most closely tied to G protein-coupled receptor signaling. When a stimulatory G protein activates the enzyme adenylyl cyclase, that enzyme converts ATP into cyclic AMP by removing two phosphate groups and forming a bond that loops back onto the ribose sugar, creating a distinctive ring structure. Cyclic AMP then diffuses away from the membrane and, in animal cells, its principal target is an enzyme called protein kinase A, which becomes active once cAMP binds it and goes on to phosphorylate a wide range of downstream proteins, a full pathway explored in the next section.

Other GPCRs, rather than activating adenylyl cyclase, activate an enzyme called phospholipase C, which cleaves a membrane phospholipid called PIP2 into two second messengers at once: inositol trisphosphate, or IP3, which is water soluble and diffuses into the cytoplasm, and diacylglycerol, or DAG, which remains in the membrane. IP3 travels to receptors on the endoplasmic reticulum and triggers the release of stored calcium ions into the cytoplasm, while DAG, together with the released calcium, helps activate protein kinase C at the membrane. Calcium ions themselves function as one of the most widely used second messengers in biology, since their cytoplasmic concentration is normally kept extremely low, so even a modest release from internal stores produces a large, easily detected relative change that many calcium binding proteins, such as calmodulin, are built to sense.

A defining feature of second messengers is that a single activated enzyme can generate a large number of second messenger molecules in a short time, since enzymes like adenylyl cyclase and phospholipase C are catalysts that turn over many substrate molecules per second rather than being consumed in a single reaction. This is the molecular basis for much of the amplification that occurs during signal transduction generally. Second messenger levels are also kept under tight control by degrading or removing enzymes: cyclic AMP is broken down by phosphodiesterase and cytoplasmic calcium is pumped back into storage, so the signal rises and falls as a controlled pulse rather than accumulating indefinitely.

Second messengers are the direct link between the receptor activation covered in the section on G protein-coupled receptors and the broader concept of signal transduction: they are what lets a single receptor-G protein interaction at the membrane become a signal that reaches enzymes, ion channels, and gene regulatory proteins throughout the cell within seconds. The next section follows the cyclic AMP pathway specifically from receptor to final cellular response, and later sections show how phosphorylation cascades triggered by second messengers and by receptor tyrosine kinases produce the large, precise amplification that makes cell signaling so effective at low ligand concentrations.
